title: The Mid-Range Is Dead. Long Live the Mid-Range.
dek: The numbers on every shot, and the one trade the league keeps refusing.
question: What does a shot return, by where it was taken?
headline: A mid-range jumper returns 0.79 points a shot; a three from 24-26 feet returns 1.04 — 31% more for one step back.
body_template: Chart every shot in the league by where it was taken and what it returned, and one comparison ends the argument before it starts: a mid-range jumper returns about {{mid_pps}} points per shot. A three from beyond the arc — {{three_band}} — returns about {{three_pps}}. Same possession, same ten seconds of work, roughly {{gap_pct}} more scoreboard for taking one step back.

That gap isn't a scheme opinion or an era aesthetic. It's the exchange rate printed on two seasons of play-by-play, and it holds across teams, lineups, and score states. Every mid-range attempt is, on average, a voluntary discount.

Here's the part most shot charts won't tell you: WHERE a player shoots from is one of the most stable, most predictable things in basketball — shot selection replicates at .97 season over season, the steadiest signal we measure. WHETHER those shots go in is one of the least — shot-making replicates at just .35. Translation: a player's diet is who they are; a player's hot streak is mostly weather. So when a broadcast praises “taking what the defense gives,” check what was given. A defense that concedes the mid-range isn't being generous. It's collecting the discount.

None of this means the shot should never exist. Late clock, mismatch, a defender's momentum — the mid-range is basketball's escape hatch, and stars keep it in the bag for exactly those moments. The honest framing: it's a tool for when the good options die, not a plan. Teams that treat it as a plan are paying a tax every trip and calling it toughness.
So read shot charts the way our engine does: selection first, results second, and streaks last. The diet tells you the future. The makes mostly tell you about last night.
